name: 夜来香 西京極店 (Yeraishan Nishikyogoku-ten)

claims.text: Wheat-based machi-chuka kitchen: noodles, gyoza, fried items and sauces share woks, fryers and prep surfaces, so cross-contamination with wheat is effectively unavoidable.
Chinese-diner cooking here relies on standard soy-based and bean-paste seasonings, which in Japan are wheat-containing; the signature mapo sauce is built on house doubanjiang and chili bean pastes.
Pork, egg and animal stocks run throughout the menu (mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, fried rice), cooked in shared woks, so no dish can be considered free of animal cross-contact.

Single-product wheat-noodle ramen shop with no gluten-free menu or published allergen handling; wheat noodles, wheat-based soy tare and a shared broth/water setup make cross-contamination effectively certain.
The defining seasoning is a soy (醤油) tare, which in a traditional Kyoto chuka soba shop is virtually always standard wheat-containing shoyu.
The single bowl is built on pork-bone and chicken broth with pork back-fat and chashu; there is no plant-based preparation and no separate vegan handling.
Built entirely on wheat: thick house-made noodles from 100% strong wheat flour ('オーション100％の極太麺'), in a shared boiling-water/noodle workflow typical of a noodle shop.
The dressing is a strong soy-based oil tare with prominent garlic ('醤油ベースのオイルだれ'), which in this style is virtually always wheat-containing shoyu.
Bowls center on pork back fat (背脂) and the standard toppings include raw/soft-boiled egg, pork fat, mentaiko mayo and cream cheese; no plant-based preparation is offered.

This is a traditional Japanese shokudo built around wheat and dashi. Udon is a wheat noodle, the signature katsudon is breaded (wheat batter) and bound in egg, and dishes are seasoned with a soy-and-dashi base. It is not suitable for celiacs or anyone needing strict gluten avoidance.

Soba is served alongside udon in the same kitchen, so even soba should not be assumed gluten-free - cross-contact with wheat noodles and shared broth is highly likely and no dedicated gluten-free handling is documented.
The broths and seasoning are soy- and dashi-based. Most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat, so the seasoning itself is a likely source of gluten across the menu.

The udon and soba broths are made from a bonito-forward blended dashi (fish-based), and signature dishes feature pork, egg, and fish. There are no documented vegan or plant-based options, and dashi runs through the menu.

This is a charcoal yakitori izakaya where skewers share a single grill and the menu leans heavily on soy-based seasonings. There is no documented gluten-free program, and cross-contamination on the shared grill should be assumed.
Even salt-only (塩) skewers, while reducing direct gluten exposure, cannot be considered celiac-safe given the shared grill surface and the pervasive use of soy sauce and tare nearby.
Yakitori glaze (tare) and soy-based seasonings are central to the menu, and most Japanese soy sauce and tare contain wheat. Tare skewers should be treated as containing gluten.

This is a chicken-focused yakitori restaurant; there is no vegan program and even non-meat items (such as grilled vegetables) are cooked on the same charcoal grill used for chicken, so cross-contact with animal products should be assumed.

Chicken is sourced fresh daily and skewers are prepared and grilled to order over binchotan charcoal, so guests can order item by item and ask about preparation; salt (塩) seasoning is available as an alternative to tare for those wanting to reduce soy/wheat exposure, though it is not gluten-free.

name: べた焼き節ちゃん (Betayaki Setsu-chan)

claims.text: This is a betayaki/okonomiyaki shop where the batter is wheat-flour based. Betayaki and okonomiyaki are cooked on a shared teppan (iron griddle) alongside other wheat-containing dishes, so gluten cross-contact on the griddle is effectively unavoidable. No gluten-free menu or preparation is documented. This restaurant should be treated as not celiac-safe.

Okonomiyaki/betayaki sauce typically contains wheat and soy, and most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat. No wheat-free sauce or soy is indicated, so assume the standard sauce and seasonings contain wheat.

Signature betayaki includes pork, fat scraps (脂かす) and raw egg, and the kitchen also grills meats, chicken (せせり) and seafood (イカ焼き) on the shared griddle. Dashi/bonito (鰹節) is typical in this style of cooking. There is no documented vegan menu, and cross-contact with animal products on the shared teppan should be expected.

This is a classic yoshoku (Western-style) house centered on wagyu hamburg steak and curry rice. Both are wheat-heavy by nature: hamburg patties typically use a breadcrumb/flour binder, the signature topping is demi-glace (a flour-thickened, slow-cooked sauce), and the curry rice is built on a wheat-flour roux. It is not celiac-safe, and no gluten-free accommodation is indicated.

The lunch menu features many breaded, deep-fried sides — shrimp fries, scallop fries, and house-made sausage — which use wheat breading and share fryer oil. There is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer, so cross-contamination is likely.

Yoshoku seasoning and demi-glace-style sauces in Japan are commonly built with soy sauce and stock-based seasonings, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No wheat-free or tamari alternative is indicated, so assume soy sauce here contains wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

The menu is built around wagyu beef, fried egg, seafood fries, and house-made sausage, with no vegan or vegetarian options indicated. The shared griddle and fryer used for meat and seafood make plant-only meals impractical here.

No information about allergy handling or allergen labeling appears on the restaurant's own pages or in diner reports. Because this is a small two-person operation cooking everything by hand to order, it is best to phone ahead and discuss any allergy directly before visiting.

It is a tiny, hands-on counter where the husband-and-wife team cook to order and the owner is known for explaining the dishes to guests — a setting where it is easy to ask questions about ingredients in person.

name: coffee grill 富久屋 (Coffee Grill Fukuya)

claims.text: This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The menu is classic Japanese yoshoku built on wheat: omurice/Fukuya Rice, multiple deep-fried breaded items (chicken cutlet, cream croquettes, assorted fried bites in the bento), and hamburg steak typically served with a flour-thickened demi-glace. Assume wheat is present throughout the kitchen and that fried items share oil and breading surfaces. No gluten-free preparation is documented.
The signature dishes themselves carry gluten risk: croquettes and cutlets are wheat-breaded and deep-fried, and the ketchup-rice dishes are commonly seasoned with sauces that can contain wheat.

As a traditional yoshoku kitchen, sauces and seasonings (demi-glace, ketchup-based and tonkatsu-style sauces) commonly include soy sauce, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Treat soy-derived seasonings as a wheat source. No wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

Not suitable for vegans. The core menu centers on egg (omelet/Fukuya Rice), pork and beef (hamburg, cutlets), seafood, and dairy (cream croquettes), and yoshoku cooking relies on butter, meat-based demi-glace, and dashi. No vegan options or separate preparation are documented; assume cross-contact with animal products throughout.
